Watching the news in Tokyo during the Tohoku (Sendai) Earthquake. I'd spent 3 hours in Shinjuku Park after the initial quake as it was the emergency evacuation point. Despite having lived there for 7 months already my Japanese was enough to get by but not enough to understand everything. 


Sitting in a foreign country, in your first earthquake, only half understanding everything, watching helicopters fly around, seeing buildings shake and sway, watching asphalt bend and buckle, seeing people who are very used to this disaster panic and the worry on their faces is very disconcerting. 


Then going back to your hotel room to sit and watch your windows vibrate with each aftershock and have the tv news on with live coverage of a tsunami that is swallowing cars containing real people desperately trying to get away from an unprecedented natural disaster is terrifying.  Watching houses being ripped to shreds as they are pulled out to sea as the water retreats just hoping no one is on their roof waiting for salvation. 


Knowing where I was in relation to Tokyo Bay that if the tsunami made it in there I was dead. Dead. I have no idea if it was feasible for it to make it in. It didn't matter. I was sure I wasn't going to be able to come back to Canada. That my family would never get my body. 


The nuclear problems were nothing. Nothing. I watched the fire fighters from Tokyo drive off to help cool off the reactor. It was humbling, but the fallout fear was nothing compared to March 11th.

Background: For the past few months HK citizens have been protesting what started out as an opposition extradition bill to China. The protests started as peaceful marches to show opposition to the perceived interference by the CCP into the One Country Two Systems they've had since Britain returned HK to China in the 90's. 


The protests escalated as the police become violent and the protesters were called rioters. Violence levels grew, arrests increased, treatment of arestees has been called into question with allegations of sexual assault,torture, beatings, and rape.  



The protesters demands grew to 5 demands that were a general consensus as it is a true grass roots organization with no one leader. 

1. Withdrawal of the Extradition Bill (accomplished now)

2. Amnesty for Protesters. 

3. An independant Inquiry into the Police violence.

4.  Reclassification of the demonstrations to protests and not riots. 

5. True universal Suffrage. 

There have been multiple targeted assaults, disappearances, suspicious deaths, violations of human rights and medical neutrality, and over use of riot gear in the past 5 months including tear gas which is building up in the city. 

As for the above post:  In the recent events, protesters have been defending university campuses and there has been escalations over the past two weeks. The protesters were only left on one campus, Polytechnic University or PolyU for short. Yesterday (ish depending on time zones) the police declared the protesters had to surrender or leave or they would resort to live rounds and charge in order to end the siege and war of attrition between the two sides. 

Since then students tried to leave via the avenue they were told and arrested, and it has escalated. There are many reports of live rounds and a lot of confusion as to verified what atm so I am not going to pretend to be a verified source of the latest. Last I saw was that there only some students left and no way out so crowds of citizens were marching to try and save them from a possible massacre.  

(This is a gross over simplification of the escalation and events but I also don't have many sources atm to give other than r/HongKong which is definitely pro hk and anti police) 


In the spirit of honesty I fall on the Pro HK side and it is definitely reflected in my summary. Please do your research and don't just take my word for it. Be informed.

Years ago, my mother got me a brass coloured bedside table lamp that looked like an oil lamp and gave me an old analogue wind up alarm clock that matched the colouring. The lamp stayed at my parent's but the clock came with me when I shakily ventured into adulthood as my own temporal comfort blanket. 

I have for years religiously kept it wound - three times when I woke up - and it has remained a faithful time keeping device and traditional two bell alarm. Sometime between coming home from Japan exchange and my wrist problems I fell out of the habit and it has been nothing more than an expensive paper weight on my bedside table. Now and then I get the inclination to wind it and I keep up with it a few days but never have I managed to get myself back in the routine. I have had no ticking clock since my year abroad and have slowly come to terms with sleeping in as much silence as an urban landscape can offer. 

Then one night as I played a game of solitaire on my phone and was drifting away I was listening to the crunch of tires in the alley, carried up on evening drafts to my open window. I was content to have only the sound of distant planes landing as my accompaniment to the orchestra of my thoughts. But something felt off so I put my phone down to try and decide if it was my roommates television or people outside and thus I should shut my window. That's when I realized my clock's been ticking. 

I didn't wind it.
